preamble: Loss of the close front vowel [i] typically affects short unstressed vowels, either word-internally (syncope) or in final syllables (apocope). Vulgar Latin syncopated post-tonic i (calidus > caldus, uiridis > uirdis, both condemned in the Appendix Probi). In Germanic, unstressed *i of the final syllable was lost after a heavy syllable: Proto-Norse gastiʀ > Old Norse gestr, Proto-West Germanic *gasti > Old High German gast. Northern Modern Greek dialects delete unstressed /i/ as part of their high-vowel loss ([ˈskoni] > [skon] 'dust'). In Trinitario Mojeño (Arawakan, Bolivia), rhythmic syncope deleted *i in weak metrical positions.

examples.note: Syncope of the unstressed post-tonic i; the Appendix Probi condemns calda for calida, and the syncopated form underlies Italian caldo and Spanish caldo.
Listed in the Appendix Probi as 'uiridis non uirdis'; the syncopated form underlies Italian and Spanish verde.
Unstressed *i was lost after causing i-umlaut of a > e; cf. Gothic gasts.
The same loss of final-syllable *i after a heavy root syllable; cf. Gothic brūþs.
West Germanic apocope of *i after a heavy syllable; Old Saxon gast and Old English ġiest show the same loss.
Old Saxon brūd and Old English brȳd likewise lost the final *i.
Northern dialects delete unstressed high vowels /i/ and /u/; in the extreme northern dialects this applies throughout the word, in mid-northern dialects only word-finally.
The vowel of the weak syllable of the first foot was deleted.
